title: Yamaha CX5M Music Computer
subtitle: The whole computer is a synthesizer
why_scout_cares: A full MSX home computer whose entire reason for existing was being a musical instrument, sold in music stores. You composed by TYPING notes into a stave editor and BASIC music macros on a QWERTY keyboard, or booting to MSX BASIC and calling CALL MUSIC. Fills the consumer instrument-as-computer-appliance category — none of the museum's ten music exhibits is a mass-market computer sold as an instrument, and none uses typing as the primary composition path. Also carries the DX7-voicing story: a computer fixing the best-selling synth's worst interface.

research.title: Yamaha CX5M Music Computer
research.overview:
The Yamaha CX5M, introduced in 1984, is an MSX-standard computer built around a Yamaha FM synthesizer. It was one of only two MSX machines ever sold in North America (alongside Spectravideo's), and it was marketed not as a computer but as a 'Music Computer' — sold in music stores, not computer shops. The machine boots to Microsoft MSX BASIC; a built-in SFG-01 module carries the 8-voice, 4-operator YM2151 FM chip (the same voice architecture family as the DX9/DX21/DX100), with stereo audio outputs, a connector for Yamaha's YK-10 music keyboard, and MIDI ports. The whole point of the machine was making music: the QWERTY computer keyboard was the primary composition instrument.

Music was made through software cartridges rather than piano-style playing. The YRM-101 FM Music Composer cartridge presented a musical-stave editing screen where the user entered notes step-time from the QWERTY keyboard — no real-time recording. The YRM-104 Music Macro cartridge made the synthesizer programmable from BASIC with commands like `_INST(1)` and `_PHRASE(1,"cdefg")`. YRM-102/502 let you program banks of 48 voices; YRM-103 was a DX7 voicing cartridge that gave the notoriously cryptic DX7 a real screen for editing patches. First CX5M units could only send MIDI out (to a DX7); the CX5M II / CX7M-128 (1986) added the SFG-05 module with MIDI input, and the FB-01 (1986) was essentially the SFG-05 in a standalone box.

The CX5M sold for about £1,000 in the UK in 1985 and was a commercial niche product that failed to crack the US market. Its cartridge software and ROMs are preserved and emulated today; a complete CX5M set is in the collection of the Musée des Instruments de Musique in Brussels, and another is held by the HomeComputerMuseum in the Netherlands.

deepDive.heading: Origins
deepDive.text: Yamaha was a founding member of the MSX consortium (launched 1983 by Kazuhiko Nishi's ASCII and Microsoft Japan) and used it to fuse its two identities: the world's dominant synthesizer maker — the DX7 shipped in 1983 — and a computer manufacturer. The CX line (CX5 in Japan, CX5F in France, CX5M international, CX11 Japan-only) were MSX machines dedicated to music and sound production. The CX5M's 1984 international release made it the canonical consumer 'music computer.'

deepDive.heading: Interaction model: composition by typing
deepDive.text: The defining interaction is step-time text entry as music composition. In the FM Music Composer, notes were placed on a stave using QWERTY keys; in Music Macro, whole phrases were typed as strings inside BASIC (`_PHRASE(1,"cdefg")`). Contemporaries described it as a daunting task — everything had to be entered via the keyboard. This inverts the Fairlight's professional graphical composition (a light pen on a pro workstation) into a consumer textual one, and it anchors the 'text keyboard as music input' tradition that runs down to Csound-style programming. The piano-style YK-10 keyboard was an optional bolt-on, not the point.

deepDive.heading: The DX7 voicing story
deepDive.text: The DX7 — the best-selling synthesizer in history — had a famously cryptic two-line LCD for programming its FM voices. The CX5M's YRM-103 DX7 Voicing cartridge connected the computer to a DX7 over MIDI and let the user edit the synth's patches on the CX5M's full screen. The machine's headline pitch to musicians was literally that a computer could fix the worst interface in electronic music.

deepDive.heading: Commercial fate
deepDive.text: MSX flopped in the US, and the CX5M became a cult collector's item. It was sold in music-trade magazines for about two years. The CX5M II (1986) added MIDI input via the SFG-05 module; the FB-01 (1986) was the SFG-05 released as a standalone desktop module. Cartridge ROM images and the SFG-01/05 firmware are preserved and emulated today via the cx5m.net archive.

team.name: Yamaha Corporation
team.note: Manufacturer; the CX line came from Yamaha's digital musical instrument group, which also produced the YM2151 'OPM' FM chip.

team.name: MSX consortium
team.note: Yamaha was a founding member; MSX BASIC 1.0 is Microsoft's, and the standard was driven by Kazuhiko Nishi (ASCII/Microsoft Japan).

team.name: Digital Music Systems Ltd
team.note: UK third-party maker of the D.M.S.1 cartridge, which added real-time 8-track sequencing of internal and external MIDI in 1985.
